title: Κύων ⟨κοιμώμενος⟩ καὶ λύκος
titleEn: The Sleeping Dog and the Wolf
part: The Sleeping Dog and the Wolf (Chambry 184)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 184. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A dog was sleeping in front of a certain farmstead.
sentences.n: ἔπαυλις is the steading — the farm buildings and yard where the stock is penned. Chambry's title supplies ⟨κοιμώμενος⟩, 'sleeping', in angle brackets: the word is his own addition to the heading, not something the manuscripts give him.

sentences.t: Λύκου δ’ ἐπιδραμόντος καὶ βρῶμα μέλλοντος θήσειν αὐτόν, ἐδεῖτο μὴ νῦν αὐτὸν καταθῦσαι.
sentences.tr: Lykou d’ epidramontos kai brōma mellontos thēsein auton, edeito mē nyn auton katathysai.
sentences.l: And a wolf having run up and being about to make him his meal, the dog kept begging him not to slaughter him now.
sentences.i: A wolf ran up and was on the point of making a meal of him, and the dog kept begging him not to kill him just yet.
sentences.n: One genitive absolute carries two participles on the same subject: Λύκου ἐπιδραμόντος … μέλλοντος. τίθημι with a double accusative is 'to make X into Y' — to make him food. μή is the regular negative with the infinitive after a verb of begging, and the imperfect ἐδεῖτο keeps the pleading going. καταθύω is to slaughter as a victim is slaughtered.

sentences.t: « Νῦν μὲν γάρ, φησί, λεπτός εἰμι καὶ ἰσχνός· ἂν δὲ μικρὸν ἀναμείνῃς, μέλλουσιν οἱ ἐμοὶ δεσπόται ποιήσειν γάμους, κἀγὼ τηνικαῦτα πολλὰ φαγὼν πιμελέστερος ἔσομαι, καὶ σοὶ ἡδύτερον βρῶμα γενήσομαι. »
sentences.tr: « Nyn men gar, phēsi, leptos eimi kai ischnos· an de mikron anameinēis, mellousin hoi emoi despotai poiēsein gamous, kagō tēnikauta polla phagōn pimelesteros esomai, kai soi hēdyteron brōma genēsomai. »
sentences.l: « For now, he says, I am thin and lean; but if you wait a little, my masters are going to hold a wedding, and I at that time, having eaten much, shall be fatter, and shall become a sweeter meal for you. »
sentences.i: « Just now, he said, I am thin and scrawny; but wait a little and my masters are going to hold a wedding, and then I shall eat my fill and be plumper, and make you a better meal. »
sentences.n: φησί is a present slipped inside the quotation — the storyteller's 'says he', which English puts in the past. ἄν here is ἐάν, and with the aorist subjunctive it makes the ordinary future condition. γάμους ποιεῖν is to hold a wedding; what interests the dog is the feast and the scraps. σοί is a dative of interest, 'for you'.

sentences.t: Ὁ μὲν οὖν λύκος πεισθεὶς ἀπῆλθε· μεθ’ ἡμέρας δ’ ἐπανελθὼν εὗρεν ἄνω ἐπὶ τοῦ δώματος τὸν κύνα καθεύδοντα, καὶ στὰς κάτωθεν πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ἐκάλει, ὑπομιμνήσκων αὐτὸν τῶν συνθηκῶν.
sentences.tr: Ho men oun lykos peistheis apēlthe· meth’ hēmeras d’ epanelthōn heuren anō epi tou dōmatos ton kyna katheudonta, kai stas katōthen pros heauton ekalei, hypomimnēskōn auton tōn synthēkōn.
sentences.l: So the wolf, having been persuaded, went away; and having come back after some days he found the dog sleeping up above on the roof, and having stood below he kept calling him to himself, reminding him of their agreement.
sentences.i: So the wolf let himself be talked round and went off; and coming back some days later he found the dog asleep up on the roof, and standing below he kept calling him down, reminding him of their bargain.
sentences.n: πεισθείς is the aorist passive of πείθω — 'having been persuaded' is how Greek says a man let himself be talked round. μεθ’ ἡμέρας, 'after days', is the idiom for a few days later. δῶμα is the flat house-roof, which one can lie on. ὑπομιμνήσκω takes the accusative of the person reminded and the genitive of the thing recalled.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ κύων· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ λύκε, εἰ τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦδε πρὸ τῆς ἐπαύλεώς με ἴδοις καθεύδοντα, μηκέτι γάμους ἀναμείνῃς. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho kyōn· « All’, ō lyke, ei to apo toude pro tēs epauleōs me idois katheudonta, mēketi gamous anameinēis. »
sentences.l: And the dog: « But, wolf, if from this point on you should see me sleeping in front of the farmstead, wait for a wedding no longer. »
sentences.i: And the dog answered: « Wolf, if from now on you should see me asleep in front of the steading, don't wait for any wedding. »
sentences.n: The Greek writes no verb of speaking — Καὶ ὁ κύων, 'And the dog', with 'said' left to be understood; the idiomatic line supplies it. τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦδε is an adverbial accusative, 'as to what comes from this point'. μηκέτι with the aorist subjunctive ἀναμείνῃς is the regular way of forbidding a single act, where a present imperative would forbid one already going on.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ φρόνιμοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὅταν περί τι κινδυνεύσαντες σωθῶσι, διὰ βίου τοῦτο φυλάττονται.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti hoi phronimoi tōn anthrōpōn, hotan peri ti kindyneusantes sōthōsi, dia biou touto phylattontai.
sentences.l: The fable shows that the prudent among men, whenever they have run a risk over something and been brought through it, guard themselves against that thing their whole life long.
sentences.i: The fable shows that sensible men, once they have come through a danger, are on their guard against that thing for the rest of their lives.
sentences.n: ὅταν with the aorist subjunctive states the general case, not one occasion. κινδυνεύω περί τι is to run a risk in the matter of something. διὰ βίου is 'through life', for as long as one lives. φυλάττονται is middle — guard themselves against — taking the accusative of what is feared.
